Sharp estimates for the convergence rate of Orthomin(k) for a class of linear systems Note: This work was supported the National Science Foundation under award number 2409951.

Journal: J. Comput. Appl. Math.
Andrei Drăgănescu Email: draga@umbc.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, 1000 Hilltop Circle, MD, 21250, Baltimore, USA Corresponding author: Corresponding author    Florin Spinu Email: fspinu@gmail.com Affiliation: New York, USA
Abstract

In this work we show that the convergence rate of Orthomin(kk) applied to systems of the form (I+ρ​U)​x=b(I+\rho U)x=b, where UU is a unitary operator and 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, is less than or equal to ρ\rho. Moreover, we give examples of operators UU and ρ>0\rho>0 for which the asymptotic convergence rate of Orthomin(kk) is exactly ρ\rho, thus showing that the estimate is sharp. While the systems under scrutiny may not be of great interest in themselves, their existence shows that, in general, Orthomin(kk) does not converge faster than Orthomin(1). Furthermore, we give examples of systems for which Orthomin(kk) has the same asymptotic convergence rate as Orthomin(22) for k≥2k\geq 2, but smaller than that of Orthomin(11). The latter systems are related to the numerical solution of certain partial differential equations.

Keywords: 
Orthomin(kk) , iterative methods
2020 MSC
65F10

1 Introduction

Originating with the work of Vinsome [1], Orthomin(kk) (k=1,2,3,…k=1,2,3,\dots) is a family of iterative methods for solving linear systems of the form

A​x=b,Ax=b, (1)

where A∈ℂd×dA\in\mathbb{C}^{d\times d} is a nonsingular, possibly non-symmetric matrix, and b∈ℂdb\in\mathbb{C}^{d}. While Orthomin has received less attention compared to other iterative methods for non-symmetric systems, it has also known some developments and extensions over time, e.g., to nonlinear systems [2], and to singular and inconsistent systems [3, 4, 5]. It has also been applied to several problems involving fluid flows [6, 7, 8].

Following [9], Orthomin(kk) can be regarded as an incompletely orthogonalized, or truncated, version of the Generalized Conjugate Residual (GCR) method, similarly to the way the Incomplete Orthogonalization Method (IOM) is related to the Full Orthogonalization Method (FOM), or quasi-GMRES to GMRES. The main attraction of truncated Krylov-space methods lies in the fact that they lead to a fixed-term recurrence, thus the cost per iteration is fixed (or bounded). The downside is that the convergence rate is not guaranteed to improve by increasing the number of terms in the recurrence; to the best of our knowledge, this fact has not been rigorously justified. We quote from [10] (p.34): “Unfortunately, no stronger a priori bounds on the residual norm are known for Orthomin(2) applied to a general matrix whose field of values does not contain the origin although, in practice, it may perform significantly better than Orthomin(1).” This is the main reason for which, in practice, GMRES is restarted after a number of steps rather than the orthogonalization process being truncated, i.e., using quasi-GMRES.

The main goal of this article is to examine the behavior of Orthomin(kk) on a family of examples, and to show essentially that for any k>1k>1 there are examples of systems where Orthomin(kk) has the same convergence rate as Orthomin(11). This is consistent with the quote above; namely, it shows that, in absence of additional assumptions on the matrix AA, no a priori bounds can be found to show that Orthomin(kk) converges faster than Orthomin(11).

2 Brief background

In this section we describe Orthomin(kk) and give a brief background on the main known convergence result. If xnx_{n} is the nthn^{\mathrm{th}} iteration and rn=b−A​xnr_{n}=b-Ax_{n} is the nthn^{\mathrm{th}} residual, the main idea is to find as xn+1=xn+xx_{n+1}=x_{n}+x, with the correction xx lying in a kk-dimensional subspace Vk(n)V_{k}^{(n)} (or (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional for (n+1)<k(n+1)<k), so that the Euclidean norm of the next residual rn+1=rn−A​xr_{n+1}=r_{n}-Ax is minimized:

‖rn+1‖2=minx∈Vk(n)⁡‖rn−A​x‖2.\displaystyle|\!|r_{n+1}|\!|^{2}=\min_{x\in V_{k}^{(n)}}|\!|r_{n}-Ax|\!|^{2}\ . (2)

The definition (2) is equivalent to

rn+1=rn−ΠA​Vk(n)​rn,\displaystyle r_{n+1}=r_{n}-\Pi_{AV_{k}^{(n)}}r_{n}\ , (3)

where ΠV\Pi_{V} is the orthogonal projection on a subspace VV. The algorithm generates a sequence of vectors p0,p1,p2,…p_{0},p_{1},p_{2},\dots, called the search directions, and for n≥k−1n\geq k-1 the space Vk(n)V_{k}^{(n)} is generated by the last kk search directions pn,pn−1,…,pn−k+1p_{n},p_{n-1},\dots,p_{n-k+1}; for n<k−1n<k-1 the space Vk(n)V_{k}^{(n)} is simply span⁡{pn,pn−1,…,p0}\mathrm{span}\{p_{n},p_{n-1},\dots,p_{0}\}. To give a precise formulation, for an initial guess x0x_{0} we initialize the residual and the initial search direction by p0=r0=b−A​x0p_{0}=r_{0}=b-Ax_{0}, and the Orthomin(kk) iteration reads

λn\displaystyle\lambda_{n} =\displaystyle= (rn,A​pn)(A​pn,A​pn),νn(j)=(A​rn+1,A​pn−j+1)(A​pn−j+1,A​pn−j+1),\displaystyle\frac{\left(r_{n},Ap_{n}\right)}{\left(Ap_{n},Ap_{n}\right)},\ \ \ \nu_{n}^{(j)}=\frac{\left(Ar_{n+1},Ap_{n-j+1}\right)}{\left(Ap_{n-j+1},Ap_{n-j+1}\right)}, (4)

pn+1\displaystyle p_{n+1} =\displaystyle= rn+1−∑j=1min⁡(k−1,n+1)νn(j)​pn−j+1,\displaystyle r_{n+1}-\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k-1,n+1)}\nu_{n}^{(j)}p_{n-j+1}, (6)

for j=1,…,min⁡(k−1,n+1)j=1,\dots,\min(k-1,n+1). Here (u,v)=∑j=1duj​vj¯\left(u,v\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_{j}\overline{v_{j}} denotes the inner product in ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}, and ‖u‖=def(u,u)|\!|u|\!|\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\sqrt{\left(u,u\right)}. The coefficients λn\lambda_{n} and νn(j)\nu_{n}^{(j)} in (4) are defined so that

rn+1⟂A​pnandA​pn+1⟂A​pn−j+1,forj=1,…,min⁡(k−1,n+1).\displaystyle r_{n+1}\perp Ap_{n}\ \ \mathrm{and}\ \ Ap_{n+1}\perp Ap_{n-j+1}\ ,\ \ \mathrm{for}\ \ j=1,\dots,\min(k-1,n+1)\ . (7)

An inductive argument shows that rn+1⟂A​pn−j+1r_{n+1}\perp Ap_{n-j+1} for j=1,…,min⁡(k,n+1)j=1,\dots,\min(k,n+1), and hence (2) holds.

Although of limited use in practice, Orthomin(kk) could be thought of as attractive mainly for two reasons. First, as with other truncated Krylov-space methods, Orthomin(kk) requires only one matrix-vector per iteration, and the additional cost (per iteration) is O⁡(k​d)O(kd) Flops; a maximum number of kk vectors need to be stored. Second, when symmetric positive preconditioners are used to produce a split preconditioning of Orthomin(kk), the preconditioned iteration can be implemented without reference to the factors of the preconditioners. This is a feature shared with preconditioned conjugate gradient (CG), as shown by Elman [11], and it allows for matrix-free preconditioning.

In terms of convergence properties, Orthomin(kk) is guaranteed to converge, for any initial guess, if the field of values11 1 The field of values or numerical range of a complex matrix AA is defined as the set of complex numbers ℱ(A)={(Au,u):u∈ℂd,||u||=1}.{\mathcal{F}}(A)=\left\{\left(Au,u\right)\ :\ u\in\mathbb{C}^{d},\ \left|\!\left|u\right|\!\right|=1\right\}\ . of the matrix AA does not contain 0. The precise convergence result and estimate shown below appears in [10] as Theorem 2.2.2, and was proved first in [12] (see elso Elman [11]) for matrices with positive definite symmetric part. We recall the following result from [10]:

Theorem 1

Assume that 0∉ℱ⁡(A)0\notin{\mathcal{F}}(A) and δ=dist⁡(0,ℱ⁡(A))\delta=\mathrm{dist}(0,{\mathcal{F}}(A)). If rnr_{n} is the nthn^{\mathrm{th}} residual in the Orthomin(kk) iteration, then

‖rn+1‖≤‖rn‖​1−δ2‖A‖2,|\!|r_{n+1}|\!|\leq|\!|r_{n}|\!|\sqrt{1-\frac{\delta^{2}}{|\!|A|\!|^{2}}}\ , (8)

where ‖A‖|\!|A|\!| is the 22-norm of the matrix AA.

We also recall from [10] the parallelism between Orthomin(1) and Steepest Descent (SD) on one hand, and between Orthomin(2) and CG, on the other. SD can only be used in connection to symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems and has an iteration of the form (5) with the search direction given by pn=rnp_{n}=r_{n}, just like Orthomin(1). However, for SD the coefficient λn\lambda_{n} is chosen so that

en+1=en−Πspan​{rn}A​en,e_{n+1}=e_{n}-\Pi_{\mathrm{span}\{r_{n}\}}^{A}e_{n}\ ,

where ΠVA\Pi_{V}^{A} is the projection on the subspace VV with respect to the AA-inner product (u,v)A=(A​u,v)\left(u,v\right)_{A}=\left(Au,v\right). Consequently, the error estimates for steepest descent are similar to the ones for Orthomin(1), and in practice the two methods converge comparably fast for SPD systems. Analogously, the sequence of search directions p0,p1,…p_{0},p_{1},\dots for CG follows a recursion that is similar to Orthomin(2), except for in CG we have

en+1=en−Πspan⁡{pn,pn+1}A​en.e_{n+1}=e_{n}-\Pi_{\mathrm{span}\{p_{n},p_{n+1}\}}^{A}e_{n}\ .

In addition, in the case of CG, the second set of orthogonality relations in (7) is replaced by the AA-orthogonality relation pn+1⟂Apnp_{n+1}\perp_{A}p_{n} (conjugate), whereas for Orthomin(2) they read A​pn+1⟂A​pnAp_{n+1}\perp Ap_{n}. Even though the superiority of CG over SD is well established and understood [9], not the same can be said about the relation of Orthomin(2) with Orthomin(1) for non-symmetric systems.

The main contribution of this article is to show that Orthomin(kk) does not perform better in general (that is, for matrices AA that satisfy 0∉ℱ⁡(A)0\notin{\mathcal{F}}(A)) than Orthomin(11). In Section 3 we consider matrices of the form A=I+ρ​UA=I+\rho U with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and UU unitary. First we show that the convergence rate of Orthomin(kk) for such systems is less than or equal to ρ\rho. Next we conjecture that, for certain examples – all involving diagonal unitary matrices UU – the asymptotic convergence rate of Orthomin(kk) is precisely ρ\rho; we support our conjecture with numerical evidence for k≥2k\geq 2 and we provide analytical arguments for k=1k=1 in Section 5, which forms the core of this article. Prior to the analysis of the convergence rate of Orthomin(1), in Section 4 we give examples of systems for which Orthomin(jj), j=2,…,kj=2,\dots,k all achieve the same asymptotic convergence rate, but converge faster than Orthomin(1).

3 The main examples

Throughout this article we denote by σ⁡(A)\sigma(A) the spectrum of a matrix AA. Furthermore, for z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} and ρ>0\rho>0 let

ℬρ​(z)¯={w∈ℂ:|w−z|≤ρ}.\overline{{\mathcal{B}}_{\rho}(z)}=\{w\in\mathbb{C}\>:\>|w-z|\leq\rho\}.

Consider the linear system

(I+ρ​U)​x=b,\displaystyle(I+\rho U)x=b\ , (9)

where 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, U∈ℂd×dU\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}} is a unitary matrix, and b∈ℂdb\in\mathbb{C}^{d}. Our goal is to assess the behavior/convergence of the ratios

qn=‖rn+1(k)‖‖rn(k)‖,q_{n}=\frac{|\!|r^{(k)}_{n+1}|\!|}{|\!|r^{(k)}_{n}|\!|}\ , (10)

where rn(k)r^{(k)}_{n} is the nthn^{\mathrm{th}} residual in the Orthomin(kk) iteration.

3.1 An upper bound

The fact that qnq_{n} is bounded above by ρ\rho is a consequence of the following result.

Theorem 2

Let A∈ℂd×dA\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}} be a normal matrix so that

σ⁡(A)⊆ℬρ​(z0)¯\displaystyle\sigma(A)\subseteq\overline{{\mathcal{B}}_{\rho}(z_{0})} (11)

with 0<ρ<|z0|0<\rho<\lvert z_{0}\rvert. The residuals rn(k)r_{n}^{(k)} obtained by applying the Orthomin(k)(k) iteration to the system (1) satisfy

‖rn+1(k)‖≤ρ|z0|​‖rn(k)‖.\displaystyle|\!|r_{n+1}^{(k)}|\!|\leq\frac{\rho}{\lvert z_{0}\rvert}|\!|r_{n}^{(k)}|\!|\ . (12)
Proof 1

Let U=ρ−1​(A−z0​I)U=\rho^{-1}(A-z_{0}I). Since σ⁡(A)⊆ℬρ​(z0)¯\sigma(A)\subseteq\overline{{\mathcal{B}}_{\rho}(z_{0})} we have σ⁡(U)⊆ℬ1​(0)¯\sigma(U)\subseteq\overline{{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(0)}. Because AA is normal it follows that UU is also normal, hence ‖U‖2≤1|\!|U|\!|_{2}\leq 1. If p0,p1,…p_{0},p_{1},\dots are the search directions of Orthomin(kk) we have

rn+1(k)=rn(k)−Πspan⁡{A​pn,…,A​pn−j}​rn(k),\displaystyle{r}_{n+1}^{(k)}={r}_{n}^{(k)}-\Pi_{\mathrm{span}\{Ap_{n},\dots,Ap_{n-j}\}}r_{n}^{(k)},

where j=min⁡(n,k−1)j=\min(n,k-1). Hence,

‖rn+1(k)‖≤‖rn(k)−v‖,∀v∈span⁡{A​pn,…,A​pn−j}.\displaystyle|\!|{r}_{n+1}^{(k)}|\!|\leq|\!|{r}_{n}^{(k)}-{v}|\!|\ ,\ \ \forall{v}\in\mathrm{span}\{Ap_{n},\dots,Ap_{n-j}\}\ .

Since rn(k)∈span⁡{pn,…,pn−j}{r}_{n}^{(k)}\in\mathrm{span}\{{p}_{n},\dots,{p}_{n-j}\}, we have

A​rn(k)∈span⁡{A​pn,…,A​pn−j}.\displaystyle Ar_{n}^{(k)}\in\mathrm{span}\{{Ap}_{n},\dots,{Ap}_{n-j}\}\ .

Therefore

‖rn+1(k)‖≤‖rn(k)−z0−1​A​rn(k)‖=ρ|z0|||U​rn(k)||≤ρ|z0|​‖rn(k)‖.\displaystyle|\!|{r}_{n+1}^{(k)}|\!|\leq|\!|{r}_{n}^{(k)}-z_{0}^{-1}Ar_{n}^{(k)}|\!|=\frac{\rho}{\lvert z_{0}\rvert}|\!|Ur_{n}^{(k)}|\!|\leq\frac{\rho}{\lvert z_{0}\rvert}|\!|{r}_{n}^{(k)}|\!|\ .

Cf. [13], if AA is normal, then ℱ⁡(A){\mathcal{F}}({A}) is equal to the convex hull σ⁡(A)\sigma({A}). Therefore, (11) is equivalent to ℱ⁡(A)⊆ℬρ​(z0)¯{\mathcal{F}}({A})\subseteq\overline{{\mathcal{B}}_{\rho}(z_{0})}. Hence, the general result (8) implies

‖rn+1(k)‖≤1−(|z0|−ρ)2(|z0|+ρ)2​‖rn(k)‖=2​ρ/|z0|1+ρ/|z0|​‖rn(k)‖.\displaystyle|\!|{r}_{n+1}^{(k)}|\!|\leq\sqrt{1-\frac{(\lvert z_{0}\rvert-\rho)^{2}}{(\lvert z_{0}\rvert+\rho)^{2}}}\>|\!|{r}_{n}^{(k)}|\!|\ =\frac{2\sqrt{\rho/\lvert z_{0}\rvert}}{1+\rho/\lvert z_{0}\rvert}\>|\!|{r}_{n}^{(k)}|\!|. (13)

The bound (12), valid for normal operators only, is sharper than (13).

3.2 Sharpness of the upper bound

To show that the estimate (12) is sharp we consider the diagonal matrices

U=diag⁡[1,ζd,ζd2,…,ζdd−1],\displaystyle U=\mathrm{diag}[1,\zeta_{d},\zeta_{d}^{2},\dots,\zeta_{d}^{d-1}]\ , (14)

where ζd=exp⁡(2​π​𝐢/d)\zeta_{d}=\exp(2\pi{\bf i}/d) is the primitive root of unity of order dd.

Conjecture 3

For all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, there exists dk∈ℕd_{k}\in\mathbb{N} and 0<ρk<10<\rho_{k}<1 so that for all ρ∈(0,ρk)\rho\in(0,\rho_{k}) and d≥dkd\geq d_{k}, the residuals rn(k)r_{n}^{(k)} obtained by applying the Orthomin(k)(k) iteration to the system (9) with UU of the form (14) and initial value x0=0x_{0}=0 satisfy

limn→∞‖rn+1(k)‖‖rn(k)‖=ρ.\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|\!|r_{n+1}^{(k)}|\!|}{|\!|r_{n}^{(k)}|\!|}=\rho\ . (15)

In this article we prove Conjecture 3 in the case when k=1k=1 (see Theorem 17 in Section 5.5). For k≥2k\geq 2, the numerical evidence in support of Conjecture 3 is quite strong, as shown in A. A consequence of Conjecture 3 is that for a given k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we can find linear systems for which all of Orthomin(jj), j=1,…,kj=1,\dots,k, achieve the same convergence rate. This establishes why there is no general result, e.g., valid for all matrices AA for with 0∉ℱ⁡(A)0\notin{\mathcal{F}}(A), showing that Orthomin(kk) converge faster than Orthomin(1). Naturally, for any system in ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}, Orthomin(dd) will converge in at most dd steps; therefore, it is necessary that dk>kd_{k}>k in order for (15) to make sense. This is not a sufficient condition, as seen from Proposition 13, where it is shown that d1≥3d_{1}\geq 3 is necessary for (15) to hold. In addition, for Orthomin(11), Conjecture 12 suggests that ρk=cos⁡(π/dk){\rho}_{k}=\cos(\pi/d_{k}), which represents the radius of the circle inscribed in the regular polygon formed by the roots of unity or order dkd_{k}. If Orthomin(11) serves as a guide, this value for ρk{\rho}_{k} may be a good choice for Orthomin(kk) as well.

3.3 Connection with numerical partial differential equations

Systems of the form (9) arise naturally in the numerical solution of partial differential equations (PDEs). Consider the steady-state advection-reaction-diffusion equation on [0,2​π][0,2\pi]

−a​u′′​(x)+b​u′​(x)+c​u​(x)=f⁡(x),a>0,c≥0,b∈ℝ,\displaystyle-au^{\prime\prime}(x)+bu^{\prime}(x)+cu(x)=f(x)\ ,\ \ a>0,\ c\geq 0,\ b\in\mathbb{R}\ , (16)

with periodic boundary conditions u⁡(0)=u⁡(2​π),u′​(0)=u′​(2​π)u(0)=u(2\pi),\ u^{\prime}(0)=u^{\prime}(2\pi). To obtain a discretization of (16) we proceed as follows: set xj=j​hx_{j}=jh, j=0,1,…,dj=0,1,\dots,d, h=2​π/dh=2\pi/d, be a uniform grid (we identify x0x_{0} with xdx_{d}, x−1x_{-1} with xd−1x_{d-1}, and x1x_{1} with xd+1x_{d+1}), and replace the derivatives in (16) with the usual centered difference formulas

−u′′​(xj)≈2​u​(xj)−u⁡(xj−1)−u⁡(xj+1)h2,u′​(xj)≈u⁡(xj+1)−u⁡(xj−1)2​h.-u^{\prime\prime}(x_{j})\approx\frac{2u(x_{j})-u(x_{j-1})-u(x_{j+1})}{h^{2}}\ ,\ \ \ u^{\prime}(x_{j})\approx\frac{u(x_{j+1})-u(x_{j-1})}{2h}\ .

The resulting discretization22 2 This particular discretization is not appropriate for advection-dominated problems. is a linear system of type (1): AA is a normal matrix with orthogonal eigenvectors χ(k)∈ℂd\chi^{(k)}\in\mathbb{C}^{d} and corresponding eigenvalues λk\lambda_{k} given by

χj(k)=exp⁡(𝐢​k​j​h),λk=−2​ah2​cos⁡(k​h)+𝐢​bh​sin⁡(k​h)+c+2​ah2.\chi^{(k)}_{j}=\exp({\bf i}kjh)\ ,\ \ \lambda_{k}=-\frac{2a}{h^{2}}\cos(kh)+{\bf i}\frac{b}{h}\sin(kh)+c+\frac{2a}{h^{2}}\ .

The eigenvalues lie on an ellipse with semi-axes 2​a/h22a/h^{2} and b/hb/h; when 2​a=h​b2a=hb this is a circle of radius b/hb/h. After further rescaling, the system can be brought to the form (9). However, as will be shown in Section 4, this example is quite relevant to the convergence study of Orthomin(k)(k) also when 2​a≠h​b2a\neq hb.

4 Further examples: normal matrices with spectra on ellipses

So far we have examined the systems (9), and we conjectured that for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we can find operators UU of the form (14) so that for all 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, Orthomin(jj) achieves an asymptotic convergence rate equal to ρ\rho. After a trivial rescaling, we restate Conjecture 3 in the following way: for any circle 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} of center z0z_{0} and radius ρ\rho satisfying 0<ρ<|z0|0<\rho<\lvert z_{0}\rvert there exists a normal matrix AA whose spectrum lies on 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} so that for all 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, the Orthomin(jj) iteration applied to the system (1) with b=(1,1,…,1)Tb=(1,1,\dots,1)^{T} and zero initial guess has an asymptotic convergence rate of ρ/|z0|\rho/\lvert z_{0}\rvert.

In this section we show numerical evidence suggesting that if we replace the circle 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} with a non-circular ellipse ℰ{\mathcal{E}} in the example above, all Orthomin(jj) with k≥2k\geq 2 achieve the same asymptotic convergence rate ρℰ\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}}, which is smaller than the asymptotic convergence rate of Orthomin(1). For the exact formulation see Conjecture 4. We remark that the discretized numerical PDE from Section 3.3 is an example of precisely such a system.

In order to make the examples very specific we first describe an ellipse ℰ{\mathcal{E}} by its semi-axes α>0\alpha>0 and β>0\beta>0, the angle θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R} between its axes and the coordinate axes, and the position u∈ℂu\in\mathbb{C} of its center:

ℰ={u+e𝐢​θ​(α​cos⁡γ+𝐢​β​sin⁡γ):γ∈[0,2​π]}.{\mathcal{E}}=\left\{u+e^{{\bf i}\theta}(\alpha\cos\gamma+{\bf i}\beta\sin\gamma)\ :\ \gamma\in[0,2\pi]\right\}\ . (17)

It is assumed that 00 does not lie on or inside ℰ{\mathcal{E}}. For d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} we consider the numbers μj∈ℰ\mu_{j}\in{\mathcal{E}} defined as

μj=u+e𝐢​θ(αcos2​π​jd+𝐢βsin2​π​jd),j=1,…,d.\mu_{j}=u+e^{{\bf i}\theta}\left(\alpha\cos\frac{2\pi j}{d}+{\bf i}\beta\sin\frac{2\pi j}{d}\right)\ ,\ \ j=1,\dots,d\ . (18)

As before, we associate to ℰ{\mathcal{E}} a linear operator

Aℰ,d=defdiag⁡[μ1,…,μd].A_{{\mathcal{E}},d}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{def}}}{{=}}\mathrm{diag}[\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}]\ .
Conjecture 4

For any ellipse ℰ{\mathcal{E}} there exists a number ρℰ∈(0,1)\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}}\in(0,1) so that the following hold:

  • (i)

    For all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} with k≥2k\geq 2, there exists dk∈ℕd_{k}\in\mathbb{N} so that for d≥dkd\geq d_{k} the ratio qn=‖rn+1(k)‖/‖rn(k)‖q_{n}=|\!|r_{n+1}^{(k)}|\!|/|\!|r_{n}^{(k)}|\!| of the residual-norm obtained by applying the Orthomin(k)(k) iteration with zero initial guess to the system

    Aℰ,d​x=(1,1,…,1)TA_{{\mathcal{E}},d}x=(1,1,\dots,1)^{T} (19)

    satisfies

    limn→∞qn=ρℰ.\lim_{n\to\infty}q_{n}=\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}}\ . (20)
  • (ii)

    If the ellipse is not circular, then ρℰ\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}} is smaller than the asymptotic convergence rate of Orthomin(1)(1).

Two facts are notable about the behavior of Orthomin(k)(k) for the systems in Conjecture 4. First, it is remarkable that the ratios qnq_{n} converge at all; indeed, we show that for k=1k=1 the sequence {qn}n∈ℕ\{q_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is convergent regardless of the choice of the numbers μ1,…,μd\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}, but for k≥2k\geq 2 the sequence {qn}n∈ℕ\{q_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} may not be monotone, and is not expected to converge in general. The second interesting fact is that all Orthomin(k)(k) with k≥2k\geq 2 achieve the same asymptotic convergence rate for sufficiently large dd. Moreover, numerical experiments show that qnq_{n} converges to the same limit ρℰ\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}} even for a random initial guess and right-hand side bb. However, in spite of the fact that ρℰ\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}} seems to be intimately related to the ellipse, currently we do not understand the nature of this connection, i.e., how to compute ρℰ\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}} using only information about ℰ{\mathcal{E}}.

We conclude this section by showing numerical evidence in support of Conjecture 4. For numerical experiments we have selected an ellipse in general position (not aligned with the coordinate axes) with α=2\alpha=2, β=1\beta=1, u=2+𝐢u=2+{\bf i}, and θ=π/6\theta=\pi/6. For d=128d=128 we solved the system (19) using Orthomin(k)(k) with k=1,2,3,4,10k=1,2,3,4,10. In Figure 1 we plot the ratios qnq_{n} for each of the solves. The data strongly suggests that for k=2,3,4,10k=2,3,4,10 we have

qn→ρℰ≈0.6891227.q_{n}\to\rho_{{\mathcal{E}}}\approx 0.6891227\ .

This approximate value (up to the first eight digits) was also obtained when solving (19) with random right-hand side and initial guess. In the particular case of Orthomin(1), we know that qnq_{n} is convergent (and increasing): numerically we find that limqn≈0.7902\lim q_{n}\approx 0.7902.

5 Convergence analysis for Orthomin(1)

The main objective of this section is to prove Conjecture 3 for k=1k=1. In Section 5.1 we show that the sequence {qn}n∈ℕ\{q_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is increasing and bounded. After stating in Section 5.2 a few technical results, we discuss in Section 5.3 examples when qnq_{n} does not converge to ρ\rho. The behavior of qnq_{n} for two-dimensional systems is presented in Section 5.4. In Section 5.5 we prove Conjecture 3 for k=1k=1.

We consider matrices of the form

A=diag⁡[μ1,…,μd],\displaystyle A=\mathrm{diag}[\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}]\ , (21)

with μ1,…,μd∈ℂ\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}\in\mathbb{C} nonzero complex numbers. Since we are interested in the evolution of the residuals, we retain only the recursive equation from Orthomin(1) that produces the residual rn=rn(1)r_{n}=r_{n}^{(1)}:

rn+1=rn−ΠA​rn​rn,r_{n+1}=r_{n}-\Pi_{Ar_{n}}r_{n}\ , (22)

with r0∈ℂdr_{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{d} being chosen arbitrarily. Recall from (4) and (5) that

λn=(rn,A​rn)(A​rn,A​rn),rn+1=rn−λn​A​rn.\lambda_{n}=\frac{(r_{n},Ar_{n})}{(Ar_{n},Ar_{n})}\ ,\ \ r_{n+1}=r_{n}-\lambda_{n}Ar_{n}\ .

Let rn=(rn1,…​rnd)r_{n}=(r_{n}^{1},\dots r_{n}^{d}) be the coefficients of rnr_{n}. We consider the finite probability measure supported at 1,…,d1,\dots,d with weights proportional to |rn1|2|r_{n}^{1}|^{2}, …, |rnd|2|r_{n}^{d}|^{2}. We will refer to it as the rnr_{n}-measure, and use the subscript nn to denote it. For instance, the expected value of a vector ξ=(ξ1,…,ξd)\xi=(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{d}) with respect to this measure is

𝔼n​(ξ):=∑k=1dξk​|rnk|2∑k=1d|rnk|2.\mathbb{E}_{n}(\xi):=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{d}\xi_{k}|r_{n}^{k}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{d}|r_{n}^{k}|^{2}}\ .

Since rn+1=rn−λn​A​rnr_{n+1}=r_{n}-\lambda_{n}Ar_{n} has coefficients rn+1k=(1−λn​μk)​rnkr_{n+1}^{k}=(1-\lambda_{n}\mu_{k})r_{n}^{k}, the following change of variable formula holds:

𝔼n+1​(ξ)=𝔼n​(ξ​|1−λn​μ|2)𝔼n​(|1−λn​μ|2),\mathbb{E}_{n+1}(\xi)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{n}(\xi|1-\lambda_{n}\mu|^{2})}{\mathbb{E}_{n}(|1-\lambda_{n}\mu|^{2})}\ , (23)

where μ=(μ1,…,μd)\mu=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}) is the vector of eigenvalues of AA. In particular,

λn=∑k=1dμ¯k​|rnk|2∑k=1d|μk|2​|rnk|2=𝔼n​(μ¯)𝔼n​(|μ|2).\lambda_{n}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{d}\bar{\mu}_{k}|r_{n}^{k}|^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{d}|\mu_{k}|^{2}|r_{n}^{k}|^{2}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{n}(\bar{\mu})}{\mathbb{E}_{n}(|\mu|^{2})}\ . (24)

κ−τ2−1≥0.\kappa-\tau^{2}-1\geq 0.

5.3 Non-convergence to ρ\rho

Let Hull⁡(ζ1,…,ζd)\operatorname{Hull}(\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{d}) denote the convex hull of ζ1,…,ζd\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{d}. This is a compact convex subset of ℂ\mathbb{C}. Since

the sequence ωn\omega_{n} cannot converge to −ρ-\rho unless −ρ∈Hull⁡(ζ1,…,ζd)-\rho\in\operatorname{Hull}(\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{d}). Since the statements limn→∞ωn=−ρ\lim_{n\to\infty}\omega_{n}=-\rho and limn→∞qn=ρ\lim_{n\to\infty}q_{n}=\rho are equivalent, we have the following.

5.4 The case d=2

Surprisingly, this case is not completely trivial either.

Proposition 13

Assume d=2d=2 and the initial vector r0∈ℂ2r_{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{2} is arbitrary, with non-zero entries. Then qnq_{n} is a constant depending on r0r_{0}, while ωn\omega_{n} is a periodic sequence with period 22. The convergence (15) for k=1k=1 does not hold in this case.

Conclusions

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we give examples of linear systems for which we conjectured that Orthomin(1), …\dots, Orthomin(kk) achieve the same asymptotic convergence rate. These examples show that, in general, Orthomin(kk) does not converge faster than Orthomin(1). We analyze in detail the convergence of Orthomin(1) and provide numerical evidence in support of our conjectures with respect to Orthomin(kk) for k>1k>1. The analysis for Orthomin(1) is fairly complicated and we do not see a straightforward way to extend the arguments to Orthomin(kk) for k>1k>1. We provide numerical evidence that certain normal operators (related to numerical PDEs) with spectrum lying on an ellipse, have the following property: Orthomin(22), Orthomin(33), etc. all have the same asymptotic convergence rate (depending only on the ellipse); moreover this is smaller than the asymptotic convergence rate of Orthomin(11). This example offers a promising path to finding improved convergence rate estimates for Orthomin(2) under additional assumptions on the spectrum/field of values of the matrix. An important question, which remains unanswered, is whether there are applications where Orthomin(kk), perhaps coupled with preconditioners, can compete with the usual iterative solvers for non-symmetric systems.

Appendix A Numerical evidence supporting Conjecture 3

In order to verify numerically the validity of Conjecture 3, we conducted several experiments with Orthomin(kk) for the system (9) with UU as in (14); the right hand side is [1,1​…,1]T[1,1\dots,1]^{T}, and the initial guess is zero, but we also conducted experiments with random right hand side and initial guess, and the outcomes were very similar. The tolerance was set at 10−810^{-8}. We report the results of computations for k∈{1,2,3,7,11,13}k\in\{1,2,3,7,11,13\}, ρ∈{0.2,0.5,0.8}\rho\in\{0.2,0.5,0.8\}, and d=16d=16 in Figure 4, d=32d=32 in Figure 5, and d=64d=64 in Figure 6, respectively, for a total 54 cases. For each case we record the residual norms and we compare the ratios qn=‖rn+1(k)‖/‖rn(k)‖q_{n}=\|r_{n+1}^{(k)}\|/\|r_{n}^{(k)}\| of successive residual norms. In Figures 4–6 we plot the quantities log10⁡|qn−ρ|\log_{10}|q_{n}-\rho| for each case.

We should point out that for Orthomin(kk) with k=1,2,3k=1,2,3 and all the values of ρ\rho and dd that we considered, we have a rapid convergence of qnq_{n} to ρ\rho. However, for d=16d=16 and k∈{7,11,13}k\in\{7,11,13\}, we notice in Figure 4 that limn→∞qn=ρ\lim_{n\to\infty}q_{n}=\rho for the smaller value ρ=0.2\rho=0.2, but this convergence does not appear to hold for ρ∈{0.5,0.8}\rho\in\{0.5,0.8\}; instead, while still relatively small (≤10−2\leq 10^{-2}), the absolute difference |qn−ρ||q_{n}-\rho| exhibits an oscillatory behavior. However, this divergent behavior appears to gradually change towards convergence as we increase dd, as shown in Figures 5–6. For d=32d=32 we notice that limn→∞qn=ρ\lim_{n\to\infty}q_{n}=\rho for all the cases, even though it appears to be slightly slower for Orthomin(13); for d=64d=64 (Figure 6) w have convergence of qnq_{n} to ρ\rho for all the value of kk and ρ\rho. This indicates that, for a fixed kk, if dd is large enough, or ρ\rho is sufficiently small, then limn→∞qn=ρ\lim_{n\to\infty}q_{n}=\rho, which is consistent with Conjecture 3.
